extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, literary authors, critics, and educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and critical criteria for judging or producing plays and poems, with attention to dramatic causation, characterization, imagery, stagecraft, and factors affecting public reception. Also guidance on authorship, recitation effects, and how reputation and publicity shape critical response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic causation / unity of cause and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The sequence of incidents in a drama should show intelligible relations of cause and effect so that the 'sense of Before and After' is perceptible and consolatory to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author faults plays in which punishments or events seem unconnected with the faults that supposedly cause them; jagged, unexplained edges in causation leave a dull under-pain. Maintain a proportion between antecedents and consequents so events feel necessary rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character and believable transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should behave and change in ways that are intelligible from what precedes them; sudden revolutions in manners without groundwork are defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of the Prior's abrupt change of manners and other sudden reversals shows that audiences infer hidden causes when character shifts are unexplained. Avoid making a character appear as a 'metamorphosed' type without prior indication; otherwise the change feels manufactured or unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid senseless borrowing and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines, images, or speech that are merely copied or senselessly plagiarised from other works (e.g., imitations of Lear or Milton) weaken the originality and coherence of a piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text denounces 'senseless plagiarism' and the 'no less senseless adoption' of other poets' fancies; borrowed phrases that don't fit the speaker or situation are especially damaging. Ensure any allusion or echo is purposeful and integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and unity of imagery and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery and figurative language should be natural to the speaker and consistent across the piece; isolated, unique images that don't resemble surrounding speech are problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Imogino's images are 'unique in the speeches of Imogino, without the slightest resemblance to anything she says before or after.' Avoid inserting striking images that have no tonal or rhetorical continuity with the character's established voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft propriety and respect for thematic material
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical representations onstage (sets, props, rituals) must suit the subject-matter and audience expectations; profane or jarring staging (e.g., profane representation of a high altar) is liable to offend or appear incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic objects to a 'profane representation of the high altar' and to incongruous stage business (a hymn being sung by chorister boys onstage in a chapel). Do not substitute sacrilegious spectacle or gratuitous props where they undermine the work's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting spectacle for intelligible drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Using mute figures, crowd business, or constant visual movement merely to give something for those who cannot hear is an inferior substitute for dramatic substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page criticises the use of 'a number of mute drawing-room persons' who exist only 'to afford something to be seen by that very large part of a Drury Lane audience who have small chance of hearing a word.' Stage business should support, not mask, the spoken drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot clarity and resolution (avoid unsolved riddles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key plot events (e.g., a child's fate) should be made intelligible to the audience unless the mystery is a deliberate, justified artistic choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic describes a disappearance treated as 'a riddle at the representation'—audiences resent important facts left indeterminate. If you leave matters ambiguous, ensure the ambiguity is artistically defensible and not mere negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit the work to its venue and audience (scale and style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages or styles that are 'metaphysical' or otherwise unsuited to the scale and conventions of large public theatres risk rejection; tailor content to the performance context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critic notes lines as unfit 'for the present state of our immense theatres' because of their metaphysical cast. Consider whether a poem or scene requires intimate performance conditions or will be lost or misread on a large public stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for recitation and performer influence on reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner and authority of recitation can strongly shape audience reception; the reciter can 'lend his own will and apprehensive faculty' to listeners and materially alter a poem's effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that enthusiastic, celebrated reciters can create temporary sympathy that inflates a poem's apparent merit, while a reader left alone may 'sink below the poem.' Do not rely solely on performance charisma to legitimize a work's intrinsic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate factors that distort critical reception (panegyric, enmity, market needs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When predicting a work's reception, subtract for undue panegyric, anticipate private enmity, and acknowledge the market's appetite for abuse or ridicule as a sales tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: adjust expectations downward from the flattering praise that encouraged publication; allow for personal enmity (even anonymous criticism) and for the necessity of a certain proportion of abuse/ridicule in reviews to secure sales. These social dynamics can explain disproportionate critical responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of reputational prejudice (labels like 'metaphysical')
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's reputation or a convenient label (e.g., 'metaphysical') can prejudice reviewers and readers against the work before assessment on its own terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recounts how prior gossip that the author was 'devoted to metaphysics' led critics to condemn works beforehand. Authors should be aware that reputation affects reception and consider strategies to counteract unfair label-driven readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and distinct expression relieve reader confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting feelings, griefs, or complex ideas in distinct, intelligible forms ('opening out our griefs') alleviates reader distress and strengthens comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that making inner states intelligible (by giving them distinct forms) is therapeutic to readers and more effective than leaving them 'shapeless' and magnified into confusion. In practice, make abstract feeling concrete through clear images and structured expression.
